summary: The narrator, badly injured and tortured, speaks with Professor Martinez while captors (the Lancer and his men) watch. The narrator reflects on whether to choose faith and trust, deciding to believe in certain people, including Arthur, Checker and themself. The narrator urges Martinez to pretend to be distressed so the captors keep the pressure on the narrator rather than anyone else, and Martinez then pleads with the Lancer to stop. The Lancer responds by striking the narrator, and the passage ends with the narrator's body seizing in pain.
one_line: A tortured narrator and Professor Martinez face the Lancer and his men, with the narrator urging Martinez to plead and draw the torture away from others.
key_facts: The narrator reflects that they did not need their past to decide who they wanted to be now.
Martinez says of faith: "I don't believe in faith" and calls it "the antithesis of evidence-based science."
The narrator decides they only need to believe in certain people: Arthur, Checker, and Myself.
The narrator says, "I had to believe I had it in me, somewhere, to do the right thing when it came down to the wire."
The narrator tells Martinez to act as if the torture bothers her so the captors will keep going on the narrator and not anyone else.
The narrator suggests Martinez tell the captors she will give them something if they stop, beg them, and then take it back.
The Lancer leans on his walking stick and asks Martinez whether she has decided to share with the class yet.
The Lancer describes the situation to Martinez as "It's in your hands" and says, "Tell me what I want to know, and we'll stop."
Martinez makes eye contact with the narrator for the first time, which startles the narrator.
Martinez says to the Lancer, "Please stop this," very slowly and softly.
The Lancer nods to his men behind the narrator, and the narrator may have screamed.
The Lancer strikes the narrator's cheek with his hand, and the narrator cannot feel it because the body is seizing.
